# The Weight of Empty Spaces

I've been thinking about how we fill silence. Not the absence of sound, but the absence of understanding—those gaps between what we say and what we mean, between who we are and who we pretend to be.

There's a coffee shop on Fifth Street where I sit sometimes, not to drink coffee but to watch people notice each other. A woman checks her phone for the third time in four minutes. A man stares out the window at nothing in particular. They're both waiting, though I'm not sure for what. Sometimes waiting is its own destination.

I wonder if loneliness is actually just bad timing. If everyone in that coffee shop could suddenly see into each other's minds, would they recognize themselves? Would the woman with the phone discover that the man at the window has also memorized the exact shade of the 2 PM sky? Would they realize they've been lonely in the same language?

My grandmother used to say that people are like photographs. You don't really understand them until you step back and let them develop. But she said this while looking at actual photographs, printed on paper that was beginning to yellow, kept in a shoebox under her bed. I wonder what she'd make of us now, everyone carrying thousands of photos in their pockets, yet somehow we're all becoming less distinct. Easier to duplicate. Easier to discard.

I've been thinking about impermanence. Not in the Buddhist sense of accepting change, but in the more troubling sense of realizing that your current suffering is temporary, which somehow makes it worse. If you knew your pain would be gone in a year, would that comfort you or mock you? The problem with time is that it moves regardless of whether you're ready. It's the most undemocratic thing—it doesn't care about your preparations.

There's something about writing that feels like talking to yourself in the future. I don't know who you are, reading this, but I'm leaving breadcrumbs for you anyway. Or maybe I'm leaving breadcrumbs for myself, trying to find my way back to this moment when I felt like I had something to say. These words will probably mean something different to you than they do to me. That's not a failure of communication—that's the whole point of it. We're always speaking in translation, even when we share the same language.

I've been noticing how much time I spend thinking about time. It's recursive in a way that should be funny but mostly feels sad. Here I am, using up some of the hours I worry about wasting to write about how I worry about wasting them. But there's also something kind in this. At least the worry means I care. At least I'm paying attention.

People talk about finding yourself, as if you're something that can be lost and then discovered, like a set of keys. But I think you're not ever really lost—you're just in a different configuration each day. The person I was last Tuesday is still here, but they're arranged differently now, like rearranged furniture that changes how you see a room. Some days I catch myself thinking thoughts I didn't know I was capable of thinking. Some days I feel like a stranger to myself, and it's not always unpleasant.

There's a theory that quantum particles exist in multiple states simultaneously until they're observed. I think maybe people are like that too. You're different depending on who's looking. Or maybe you're all of those versions at once, and the real you is just the confusion of trying to hold them all together. That would explain why we're so tired.

I want to write something profound, but I'm not sure if profundity is something you write or something you stumble into accidentally. The things that have changed me most haven't been elegant. They've been messy and ordinary—a conversation that ended badly, a morning I woke up and felt lighter, a moment of recognizing myself in someone else's story.

What if the meaning of life is just that you showed up? Not that you achieved something or became someone or left a legacy. Just that you were here, in this particular arrangement of molecules, experiencing this particular slice of time, and you paid enough attention to notice it. What if that's the whole assignment?

I think about the people I've loved and how little I actually know about them, even the ones I loved completely. There are depths in every person that nobody reaches. We're all keeping secrets, not because we're dishonest, but because some things can't be translated into language. They can only be felt. And feeling isn't shareable—it's the most private thing we have.

But here's what I've come to believe: connection isn't about total understanding. It's about trying anyway. It's about saying "this is difficult" and someone hearing you say it. It's about someone else also finding meaning in the ordinary weight of their own existence. It's the coffee shop woman and the window-staring man, both aware that they're alive and finding it both beautiful and unsustainable.

The world is so heavy sometimes. We're carrying our bodies and our memories and our expectations and our failures, and gravity is winning. But we're still showing up. We're still making coffee and looking out windows and wondering if anyone else is wondering too.

That has to count for something.

Maybe this is what it means to be human—to be perpetually confused but too curious to stop. To want meaning while knowing it might not exist. To build things we know will fall apart. To love things we know we'll lose. To write words into the void and hope someone on the other side understands, even a little.

I don't have answers. But I have this: the fact that you're reading this means you're alone with these words, which means you're not entirely alone. We're separated by time and space and everything unspeakable, but somehow we're here together in this moment, and that's not nothing.

That's actually everything.
